name: Wandering Jew
description: Wandering Jew (Tradescantia zebrina) is a common, colorful trailing houseplant. While not severely toxic, it can cause mild discomfort for cats. The primary issue is the plant's sap, found in its leaves and stems, which contains compounds that can irritate a cat's skin and digestive system. The most common reaction occurs when a cat's skin comes into contact with the sap from a broken stem or leaf. This can cause a skin reaction called dermatitis, which may appear as redness, itchiness, or a rash. This is usually mild and localized to the area of contact. If a cat chews on the plant, the sap can irritate the mouth and stomach, leading to symptoms like drooling, pawing at the mouth, mild vomiting, or diarrhea. These signs are typically not serious and resolve on their own. If skin irritation or stomach upset continues, it is best to consult a veterinarian.
safetyNotes: Toxic compounds: irritant sap compounds throughout the plant; sap is released when leaves or stems are broken
Mechanism: sap causes contact dermatitis; ingestion causes direct GI mucosal irritation
Symptoms: skin redness or rash from contact; vomiting, diarrhea, drooling from ingestion
The trailing purple-silver leaves are visually appealing and accessible when plants hang — relocate away from cats
Symptoms are mild and usually self-limiting; rinse affected skin with water and consult your vet if GI symptoms persist

symptoms.name: Mild vomiting, drooling, and/or diarrhea
symptoms.notes: This is generally a minor gastrointestinal upset that usually resolves on its own1. You can help by cleaning the cat's mouth with water, but you should consult a veterinarian if the vomiting becomes frequent.

symptoms.name: Skin redness or itch
symptoms.onset: Occurs after prolonged physical contact with the plant's sap
symptoms.notes: If the sap gets on your cat, you should clean it off their fur and skin with water1. While usually a minor irritation, you should consult a veterinarian if the skin reaction appears severe.
